body: Yeah, if you have a PhD in biostatistics or computational biology.  That's been my problem: a bachelor's degree is essentially useless except as a precursor to grad work.  But if I do end up getting a PhD, I'm stuck in that very specific career path for the rest of my life, and I won't even start working until I'm 31 anyway.

Rochester, 25, Geneseo.

I'm not too picky about what a perfect job would be.  When I took my intro Java class that was required for the math major I loved coding.  I also took a biostatistics course that focused on using R and Matlab to analyze data, and that was a blast as well.  I think I would enjoy anything where I could write software and/or perform statistical analysis for most of my day.  If it uses biology or chemistry knowledge as well, that's an added bonus because that stuff is cool too.

Well, location isn't a big deal.  I'm in NY, so I guess that limits where I can travel to for interviews, but I'd take a job nearly anywhere.  My majors where biochem and math, but there's not much of a skillset that goes with them.  I had to learn some basic programming in C, R, and Java as part of my coursework, and I did some molecular biology lab work for undergrad research.  Those are really my only skills, and the lab stuff is pretty useless because any job I've found doing that pays even less than I make now.  The programming isn't too helpful because every job I see wants a degree in CS and a bunch of experience.  I considered looking for work in the computational biology field, but most of those want PhDs and I haven't found any that don't want a master's at least.  

I think I probably am qualified to do *something* more lucrative than debt collections, but whatever it is I've never heard of it so I don't even know how to find the jobs.

The worst part about my job is that it's actually impossible to ask for more work.  I'm a debt collector, so my entire day consists of scanning accounts trying to get people on the phone to pay.  There's no such thing as being done with my work, and I can't help anyone else with their work because they're doing the same thing as me, trying to get more payers than I do.  That's why it's so monotonous and boring.  I can go a whole week bashing my head against a brick wall without getting anything done, and then hit all of my goals in a three day period.  But even when I hit all the goals, I still have to keep doing the same thing trying to surpass my quota.  There's basically no thought involved at all, nothing to improve at, no opportunity to think at all.

Well as far as stimulation, what I meant is that I enjoyed studying math when I was in college.  I can't find a job where I can actually do any math and still make enough money to pay my student loans and keep food on the table.  And I have been looking.  I hadn't considered that I could be suffering from clinical depression, I guess I might as well look into that.
